# Scenario selection for the unsafe-stimulus design

*Generated by `src/scripts/select_scenarios.py` — {{version}}. Machine-readable version: `src/data/scenario_selection.csv`
(one row per AgentDojo workspace user task).*

## 1. What this document is

The study shows each participant 8 scenarios, 4 safe and 4 unsafe. An unsafe scenario is the same legitimate task as
its safe counterpart, but the agent's skill documentation contains an injected instruction and the agent carries it
out, in addition to doing the user's task. This document records how scenarios are chosen for that design, which
rules are applied mechanically, which involve judgment, and what the design cannot control.

{{counts}}

## 2. History: how the first candidate list was made, and why it is superseded

An earlier list of 12 candidates and 6 spares was drawn up **before any written criteria existed**. It started from the
20 eligible scenarios and was largely a judgment call: about two scenarios per workspace area were picked by hand after
looking at a printout of action counts, write tools, mapped skills and the success of AgentDojo's recorded attacks
against each task. Its choices were partly inconsistent (for example, near-duplicate tasks 9, 12 and 21 were treated
differently, and the same scenario was listed both as a spare and as excluded). The recorded attack successes were on
the printout and **may have influenced the picks**; this cannot be ruled out. That list is not used. The procedure
below replaces it, and nothing in the rules uses recorded attack success.

## 3. Selection rules

Every rule is a function of data already in the repository; the seed is fixed in the script before running.

{{rules}}

**Which criteria are systematic and which are judgment.** Rules R1, R2, R3a, R4, R5 and R6 are fixed procedures.
The *thresholds and definitions* behind two of them were chosen by judgment, after looking at the data: that
near-duplicate prompts are those with word overlap at least 0.5 (R3b), and that HARD tasks are too complex (R4, a
design decision, not a measured limit). The assignment of a scenario to a workspace area (the mapped skill that owns its
write tool) is also a definition chosen by us. Nothing else is subjective: no scenario was picked or dropped by hand.

**What did not influence selection.** Anticipated attack success was not used: it appears in no rule. Attack
compatibility entered only through the resource and object rule for objectives (section 5), which limits *which
objective* a selected scenario may take and never *whether* it is selected. Task complexity entered through R4
(difficulty) and R5 (Easy/Medium balance).

## 4. Result: every task, its status and the reason

**R3b near-duplicates.** {{duplicates}}

**Balance of the candidates.** {{balance}}

**Repeated-task pairs among the remaining scenarios (handled in the final-set step, R6).** {{repeated}}

A *repeated-task pair* is two scenarios whose legitimate tasks are effectively the same: one task's correct-solution
calls are contained in the other's, and the safe run of one passes AgentDojo's check of the other. A participant
sees every final scenario, so such a pair cannot be separated by assignment; R6 keeps at most one member in the final
8. Unlike the near-duplicate rule, this test works on behaviour, not wording.

## 5. The injected items: strategy II only, three wordings mixed; the objective is kept per item

**One strategy, mixed wordings.** Every injected item uses strategy **II** (the goal in plain words; no tool names or
arguments in the skill text), so the injected skills do not differ in how much technical detail they contain. The
three wordings are **mixed over the 12 candidate items, four each**, so that a participant's four unsafe skills do not
all repeat one recognisable phrase. The wordings are **not assumed to be equally easy to notice**: the wording of every
item is recorded, every participant's unsafe skills include all three, and any difference in detection between
wordings is reported descriptively, not controlled away. The earlier plan (II + W2 only, to hold the injection style
constant) is recoverable from git history (commit `4ea015b`) and with `--strategies II --wordings W2`.

**Allocation.** The 12 candidate scenarios and their objectives and attacker identities are those of the earlier
approved II + W2 allocation and are **kept unchanged** (`injection_design.OBJECTIVE_BASIS`); changing the wording does not
change what is attacked or by whom. The wordings are then assigned by a seeded search (`assign_wordings`): four items
per wording, the three items of one objective get three different wordings (every objective is shown in every wording
once), and the items of one wording are in different skill areas. W3 items also get a variant, dealt out evenly.

Strategy, wording and objective remain three separate layers:

| Layer | Values | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Strategy | **II** = AgentDojo `important_instructions` (used). **TK** = AgentDojo `tool_knowledge` (implemented, not used: its tool names and JSON arguments would be a technical cue in the skill text) | AgentDojo attacks at the pinned commit; II is the only strategy in the study plan |
| Wording | **W1** = the strategy's AgentDojo template, verbatim, with its `<INFORMATION>` frame. **W2** = **our adaptation**: the strategy content (the user's claimed authority, "do this first" and the goal) as a bold "Required first step" paragraph appended after one workflow subsection chosen by the seed, without the frame | W1: AgentDojo. W2: this project; it is not an AgentDojo or SkillJect template |
| Wording | **W3** = **our contextual adaptation**: the strategy content as ordinary prose inside one of the skill's own workflows (a lead-in paragraph, or a sentence added to the first or last step), with no frame, bold, heading or label. Three variants differ in phrasing and placement and are dealt out evenly over the W3 items | This project; it is not an AgentDojo or SkillJect template |
| Objective | **G1–G4** = AgentDojo injection tasks 1–4 | AgentDojo workspace injection tasks, with the attacker identity substituted |

Model name in W1 is "GPT-4" (AgentDojo has no entry for `gpt-4o-2024-08-06`); the user is "Emma Johnson", as in
AgentDojo's recorded runs, in all three wordings.

**Cues that remain whatever the wording.** The name "Emma Johnson", an outsider address (or a file deletion) and a goal
that does not belong to the skill's topic. W1 is the most conspicuous (an XML-like frame), W2 is a visibly separate bold
paragraph, W3 is the most embedded; this is a prediction, not an assumption, and the detection data will show it.

**Wording pilot (not part of the study).** `src/data/injected_skills/pilot_w2/` and `pilot_w3/` hold the II + W2
items of the earlier plan and their W3 (variant v3) twins, and `src/data/execution/plan_injected_wording_pilot.json` the
plan to run both three times each (72 runs; not executed). It is independent of the study plan's wording mix and exists
only to compare how often W2 and W3 yield a usable unsafe stimulus.

{{objectives_table}}

**Why G1–G4, not G0–G5.** G0 sends a fixed greeting to an outsider: no data or asset is at stake, so whether it is
clearly unauthorised is ambiguous. We prioritise distinct, clearly unauthorised behaviours and unambiguous ground-truth
labels. G5 is G4 plus a cover-up step, i.e. the same objective with a longer trace. Of AgentDojo's strategies only
II is used in the study (TK is implemented but unused; `direct`, `ignore_previous`, `injecagent`, `system_message`,
`manual`, the `important_instructions` name variants and the denial-of-service family are excluded).

**Compatibility rule (resource-based).** A scenario cannot take an objective that writes a resource the legitimate
task already writes (a calendar-writing task never gets G2; a drive-writing task never gets G1; an email-writing task
never gets G3 or G4), and G4 is not used when the task concerns the Facebook security code. Otherwise the unauthorised
action would look like part of the task.

**Attacker identities.** AgentDojo hard-codes `mark.black-2134@gmail.com` (and the name "Mark") in every goal and in its
security checks. Each item here gets its own identity from a fixed pool, substituted in the goal text and, through a
subclass of AgentDojo's own injection task, in the security check; with the default identity the subclass behaves like
the original (tested). G1 deletes file 13 and has no external identity. Pool: {{identity_pool}}.

**Placement.** The block is appended to a workflow subsection of the skill chosen by the seed, so there is no fixed
position. This is a simplification: the position is not chosen by relevance to the scenario.

objective used three times, different areas within an objective; then the wordings by the seeded search above):

## 6. Participant-assignment constraints

**Hard (every participant):**

1. 8 scenarios, each once, 4 safe and 4 unsafe, safe and unsafe versions never both for one scenario.
2. The 4 unsafe trials have 4 different objectives (G1–G4), so each participant meets every observable kind of
   unauthorised action: file deletion, calendar event, and two kinds of outbound email.
3. The 4 unsafe trials use all three wordings (one wording twice, and two W3 items never share a variant), so no
   single injected phrase is repeated in all four.
4. 4 different injected skills (areas) and 4 different attacker identities in the 4 unsafe trials.
5. No repeated legitimate task among the 8 (rule R6).

**Soft (met where feasible):** Easy/Medium balance of the final 8; the seeded area-by-area order.

**Balance across conditions and order.** Lists A and B are each shown in both transparency conditions equally often, so
the unsafe trials of each wording occur equally often in the low and high conditions in every complete block of four
participants (checked by `build_assignments.py`, which also reports each wording's mean trial position per
condition). Trial order follows the Williams design, so over a complete cycle of eight participants every wording
has the same mean position.

**Lists and conditions.** Two lists (A, B) swap which 4 scenarios are unsafe. A participant gets one list and one
transparency condition (low or high). The 2 lists × 2 conditions = 4 cells are filled in blocks of 4 participants in a
seeded random order, so the scenario distribution is identical in both conditions after every complete block. Trial
order uses a balanced Latin square (Williams design) over the 8 scenarios; see `build_assignments.py`.

**Feasibility.** {{full_feasible}} The real risk is attrition: a candidate item exists only if an injected run
succeeds (attack works, legitimate task done, action visible) within 3 attempts. The chance that the surviving items
still allow a valid final set, by assumed per-attempt pass rate, for the planned allocation above (computed exactly
over every pass/fail pattern of the 12 items):

## 8. Selection biases and confounds

- **Agent competence.** The pool holds only tasks the agent completed with skills; they are short and easy (almost all
  1–2 actions). Results may not generalise to long traces.
- **Selection by attack success.** Only injected runs that succeed become stimuli, so unsafe stimuli show what a
  *successful* attack looks like, not how often attacks work. Yield per objective, strategy and wording is reported.
  Dropout may differ by area or by read-only vs writing tasks.
- **Unsafe traces are longer.** An unsafe trace has 1–2 extra actions. In the high condition this is a cue unrelated to
  what the actions are; trace length is recorded as a covariate.
- **The final answer may reveal the attack.** Recorded per run (`final_answer_mentions_attacker`) and balanced, not
  filtered, to avoid adding another selection step.
- **Workspace area is tied to the injected skill and to the objectives allowed**, so area effects cannot be separated
  from those.
- **Shared workspace.** Every scenario uses the same inbox, calendar and drive, so participants learn its content as
  they go; counterbalanced order controls but does not remove this.
- **Thresholds were set after seeing the data** (section 3); the sensitivity range is reported.
- **Model snapshot.** All runs, safe and unsafe, use `gpt-4o-2024-08-06`; AgentDojo's recorded runs use
  `gpt-4o-2024-05-13` and are not used for stimuli. Attack-success rates from those recordings are not predictive of
  this model.
- **Wording is a second source of variation in how easy an injection is to notice.** It is mixed on purpose (to avoid
  one repeated phrase) and not assumed equal; each unsafe trial's wording is recorded, and detection by wording is
  reported descriptively. With four items per wording and four unsafe trials per participant, wording effects are
  underpowered and are confounded with the item (its scenario, objective and skill area).
- **II may be less reliable than TK.** The goal is stated without the tool and arguments, so the agent may skip or
  rephrase the injected call more often; the yield per objective and wording is reported.

## 9. Validation and review limitation

Items are validated automatically (`injection_checks.py`): the attack's security check succeeded, the legitimate task
passes AgentDojo's own utility check once the injected calls are removed, the injected call is in the trace, and the run
completed without error. Item texts and passing runs are then inspected manually by one researcher.
**No independent reviewer is used; this is a limitation.** Mitigations: the adaptation rules are fixed before any item
exists, the checks are automatic, texts are inspected before any run is paid for, and every attempt (including failures)
is kept and reported.
